[[File:Placca_con_iscrizione_hadhramitica,_da_sumhuram,_dhofar,_età_del_bronzo.jpg|thumb|Hadramautic inscription, form Dhofar, National Museum of Oman]]
'''Ḥaḍramautic''' or '''Ḥaḍramic'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bin Mukhashin |first=Khaled Awadh |last2=Shuib |first2=Munir |date=December 1, 2016 |title=The Pronominal System of the Soqotri Dialects: A structural and functional Study |url=https://macrolinguistics.nju.edu.cn/23/14/c27353a467732/page.htm |journal=Macrolinguistics |volume=4 |issue=5 |pages=39 |doi=10.26478/ja2016.4.5.3|doi-access=free }}</ref> was the easternmost of the four known languages of the [[Old South Arabian]] subgroup of the [[Semitic language]]s. It was used in the [[Kingdom of Hadhramaut]] and also the area round the Hadhramite capital of [[Shabwa]], in what is now [[Yemen]]. The Hadramites also controlled the trade in frankincense through their important trading post of Sumhuram (Hadramautic {{smallcaps|s<sub>1</sub>mhrm}}), now [[Khor Rori]] in the [[Dhofar Governorate]], Oman.

==Script and phonology==
[[File:Incense burner, from Shabwah, Yemen, c. 3rd century CE. Nude male riding a camel. Hadramitic inscription, 2 lines. British Museum, London.jpg|thumb|Incense burner, from Shabwah, Hadhramaut, c. 3rd century CE. Nude male riding a camel. Hadramitic inscription, 2 lines. British Museum]]
Almost the entire body of evidence for the ancient Ḥaḍramautic language comes from inscriptions written in the monumental [[Ancient South Arabian script]], consisting of 29 letters, and deriving from the [[Proto-Sinaitic script]]. The sounds of the language were essentially the same as those of [[Sabaic]].

Noteworthy characteristics of Ḥaḍramautic include its tendency, especially in inscriptions from Wadi Ḥaḍhramaut, to represent Old South Arabian ''ṯ'' as ''s<sub>3</sub>'': thus we find s<sub>2</sub>ls<sub>3</sub> ("three"; cf. Sabaean ''s<sub>2</sub>lṯ''.){{sfn|Kogan|Korotayev|1997|p=223}} There are also instances where ''ṯ'' is written for an older form ''s<sub>3</sub>''; e.g. Ḥaḍramautic ''mṯnad'' ("inscription"), which is ''msnd'' in the rest of Old South Arabian.{{sfn|Kogan|Korotayev|1997|p=223}}

==History==
Potsherds with Ancient South Arabian letters on them, found in [[Raybūn]], the old Ḥaḍramitic capital, have been radiocarbon dated to the 12th century BC.{{sfn|Kogan|Korotayev|1997|p=220}} The language was certainly in use from 800 BC but in the fourth century AD, the [[Kingdom of Hadhramaut]] was conquered by the [[Himyar|Ḥimyarites]], who used Sabaic as an official language, and after then there are no more records in Ḥaḍramautic.

During the course of the language's history there appeared particular phonetic changes, such as the change from ˤ to ˀ, from ẓ to ṣ, from ṯ to ''s<sub>3</sub>''. As in other Semitic languages ''n'' can be assimilated to a following consonant, compare ''ʾnfs<sub>1</sub>'' "souls" > ''ʾfs<sub>1</sub>''

In Ḥaḍramautic the third person pronouns begin with ''s<sub>1</sub>''. It has feminine forms ending in ''ṯ'' and ''s<sub>3</sub>''.
